parole.significato: used to form masculine nouns (often of French origin) that represent a person who makes or sells a specified article; -…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French -ier, from Latin -arius. Doublet of the inherited suffix -aio and -aro. Cognate with Sicilian -eri.
Borrowed from Old French abandoner.
Borrowed from Old French achevalchier, derived from chevalchier (“to ride”).
Borrowed from Old French hachete.
Borrowed from Old French adober.

parole.significato: to arrange (to put into an orderly sequence or arrangement)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French aisier, derived from aise, alternative form of eise (“ease”).
From Old French aire (“appearance, semblance”). Doublet of are.
Possibly from Old French alumer. By surface analysis, a- (“to, towards”) + lume (“light”) + -are.

parole.significato: to add gold or silver to pigments in order to make (a painting, usually a miniature) shine
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French enluminer.
Calque of Old French appointer (“to settle a deal”).
Borrowed from Old French archier. By surface analysis, arco + -iere.
From Old French arlot.
Borrowed from Old French hernois, herneis (“battle equipment”), likely a borrowing from an Old Norse *hernest, derived from herr (“army”) + nest (“equipment”).
Borrowed from Old French atraper, ultimately derived from Frankish *trappa (“trap, snare”).
From avviso + -are, or borrowed from Old French aviser.
Borrowed from Old French avis.
Likely borrowed from Old French hache (“axe”), from Vulgar Latin *happia (“axe, hatchet”), borrowed from Frankish *happjā (“axe”), from Proto-Germanic *hā̆bjǭ or *hē̆bjǭ (name of some sort of tool).
Borrowed from Old French bagage.
Borrowed from Old French bai, or Old Occitan, ultimately from Latin badius.
Borrowed from Old French bald, from Frankish *balþ, from Proto-Germanic *balþaz. Cognate with Old English beald and Sicilian baudu. More at English bold.
From Old French baillie.
Borrowed from Old French bailif, baillif, from Vulgar Latin *baiulivus, from Latin baiulus. Doublet of balì.

Uncertain. * From Old French balle, from Medieval Latin balla, from Frankish *ballu. * From Lombardic *palla, *balla. Both etymologies ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ballô, *balluz (“ball”). Doublet of palla. Cognate with Sicilian baḍḍa, whence the dialectal doublet badda.

parole.significato: hinny (hybrid of a male horse and a female donkey)
parole.testo: From barda, from Old French barde (“horse armor”), + -otto.

parole.significato: a large barrel used to preserve pickled fish
parole.testo: From Old French barillon.
Borrowed from Old French baron. First attested in the 13th century.
Borrowed from Old French batel. Compare Spanish, Galician, and Portuguese batel.
From battere + -eria or borrowed from Old French baterie.
Borrowed from Old French baviere.
From Old French bersail (“target for an arrow”), from berser (“to hunt with bow and arrow”), from Latin vervēx (“wether, kind of goat; blockhead, idiot”).
Borrowed from Old French blasmer. Doublet of bestemmiare and blasfemare. Cognate with Sicilian jastimijari.

Borrowed from Old French bedel (“policeman”), from Frankish *bidil (“candidate, volunteer”), from Proto-Germanic *bidilaz (“seeker”), from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną (“to ask, beseech”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰidʰ- (“to command”), merging with Frankish *budil (“messenger of justice”), from Proto-G
From Old French briba, probably ultimately from Celtic; see also Breton breva.

parole.significato: a bag, a pouch, especially one which opens longways
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old French bolge, bouge, from Late Latin bulga (“wallet, purse”) (or less likely directly from an adjectival form bulgea), from Gaulish bolgā, from Proto-Celtic *bolgos (“sack, bag”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”).
From Old French debonaire, de bon aire (“of good disposition”). Compare French débonnaire and English debonair.

From Old French bordel (“small hut, cabin; brothel”), diminutive of bord, from Medieval Latin bordellum, from Frankish *bord (“board”), from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board, table”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰr̥dʰ-o- (“board”), suffixed zero-grade form of *bʰer-edʰ- (“to cut”), suffixed form of *bʰe
From the verb bottare, from Old French boter (“to strike”), from Frankish *buttan, from Frankish *bautan (“to hit, strike”).
Borrowed from Old French breche, ultimately of Germanic origin.
Borrowed from Old French bresme. See French brème.
Borrowed from Old French brifaut.
Borrowed from Old French brocher.
Borrowed from Old French broche (whence French broche).
Borrowed from Old French brouiller (modern French brouiller (“to confuse”).
Borrowed from Old French brunir.
Borrowed from Old French burre, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτυρον (boúturon). Doublet of butirro.
Borrowed from Old French boiste, whence French boîte (“box”). Derived from Medieval Latin buxida, inflected form derived from Latin buxētum (“boxwood plantation”), from Latin buxus (“boxwood”).

parole.significato: to throw, to toss, to fling, to chuck, to sling
parole.testo: From Old French bouter (“to strike”), of Germanic origin. Compare Neapolitan vottare and Sicilian vottare.
From cammello + -otto, on the model of Old French chamelot.
From Old Italian cangiare, borrowed from Old French cangier, changier. Doublet of cambiare. Parallel borrowing with Sicilian cangiari, Spanish canjear, English change.

parole.significato: butchered meat; animals which are to be slaughtered
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French charnage.
From Old French chaston, chastun, from Frankish *kastō (“box”, “case”), from Proto-Germanic *kastô (“vessel”, “container”), extended form of *kasą, *kazą.
From Old French chalemel (whence French chalumeau), from Late Latin calamellus, from Latin calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos).
Likely from Old French cisel, with adaptation to Italian -ello and perhaps influence from cesoia (“shears”). First attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Old French chalde (“warm”).
Borrowed from Old French chamoire, itself from Late Latin camoria (“a disease of horses”).
Calque of Old French couard, from cue (“tail”). By surface analysis, coda (“tail”) + -ardo.
Borrowed from Old French conestable.
From Old French congiet, from commeātus (whence also Italian commiato).

parole.significato: county (territory of a count or countess)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French conté, from Latin comitātus. Doublet of contado. The modern sense of an administrative division is a semantic loan from English county.

parole.significato: contention, quarrel, contest, argument, dispute, debate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French contention or contençon or Latin contentiōnem. By surface analysis, contendere + -zione.
Borrowed from Old French cointe (“known, courteous, refined”), from Latin cognitus.

Borrowed from Old French cointe (“known, courteous, refined”), as with Etymology 3, but crossed with Latin cōmptus (“adorned, ornamented; arranged; dressed”), perfect passive participle of cōmō (“to arrange, to dress, to adorn”).
Borrowed from Old French cornemuser.

parole.significato: to upset, to anger, to irritate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French corocier, corucier, from Vulgar Latin *corruptiāre, from Latin corruptus, perfect passive participle of corrumpō (“to corrupt”). Doublet of crucciare.
Borrowed from Old French corsage in 1266.

parole.significato: a horse with its ears and tail docked
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French courtaud (“having a docked tail”), derived from court (“short”).
Borrowed from Old French cucu, imitative of the call.

parole.significato: a male cousin (son of one’s uncle or aunt)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French cosin, cousin, from Latin cōnsobrīnus. Doublet of consobrino.
Borrowed from Old French coissin or Old Occitan coisin, from Vulgar Latin *coxīnum, *cossīnum, from Latin coxa (“hip; thigh”).
Borrowed from Old French daine, daim, from Late Latin dāmus, from Latin dāma.
Borrowed from Old French damoisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella. Doublet of donzella.
From Old French damage, Old Occitan damnatge, from Vulgar Latin *damnāticum, derived from Latin damnum (“damage”).
Semantic loan from Old French dalphin, from Latin delphinus.
From Old French demaine (“holdings”), from Latin dominium.
Borrowed from Old French disner, from Vulgar Latin *disieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnāre (“to fast”).
Borrowed from Old French defaute.
Borrowed from Old French faleise, from Frankish *falisa, from Proto-Germanic *falisaz (“rock, cliff”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelis-, *pels- (“rock, cliff”).

From Old French fard (“make-up, cosmetics”), from farder (“to apply make-up, use cosmetics”), from Old Frankish *farwidōn (“to dye, colour/color”), from Proto-Germanic *farwiþōną (“to colour/color”), from *farwō (“colour/color”).
Borrowed from Old French flanc (“flank, side”).
Borrowed from Old French fiée, from Vulgar Latin *vicāta, from Latin vicis (“time, turn, instance”). Doublet of vicata, which was inherited.
From Old French fieu (“fief”), from Frankish *fehu, from Proto-Germanic *fehu, from Proto-Indo-European *péḱu (“livestock”).
Perhaps borrowed from Old French forger.
Borrowed from Old French formage, from Medieval Latin fōrmāticum, from Latin fōrma (“mould/mold”). Compare modern French fromage.

parole.significato: to supply, to provide, to furnish, to give, to yield
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French fornir, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *frumjan (“to complete, execute”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną (“to further, promote”), from Proto-Indo-European *promo- (“front, forward”). Compare French fournir, Catalan fornir, Spanish and Portuguese fornecer, English furnish.
Borrowed from Old French forsené.

parole.significato: French (of, from or relating to France)
parole.testo: From Francia + -ese. Borrowed from Old French franceis.

parole.significato: a curl of tape used as a decoration
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French frape, of uncertain origin.
Borrowed from Old French fleche, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia, of Frankish origin.
Borrowed from Old French flote; cf. modern French flotte.
Borrowed from Old French gab, from Old Norse gabb.
Borrowed from Old French gale (“rejoicing”), from galer (“to rejoice”).
Borrowed from Old French galoper
Borrowed from Old French galop, from galoper (“to gallop”).
From Old French garant, probably from Frankish *werênd, *warjan, akin to German gewähren (“to grant”) and Old High German wërênt.
Borrowed from Old French jergon, jargon.
Borrowed from Old French jaque.
From Old French jaquet (compare modern French jaquette, English jacket, Portuguese jaqueta, Spanish chaqueta). By surface analysis, giacca + -etta.
Borrowed from Old French jalne (variant of jaune), from Latin galbinus. Crime fiction sense is in reference to the yellow covers of a series of mystery novels published by Mondadori from 1929.
Borrowed from Old French gibet, probably from Frankish *gibb (“forked stick”).
Borrowed from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium. Doublet of gaudio. Cognate with Sicilian gioja.
From Old French joiel, a form of jouel (“jewel”).
Borrowed from Old French joieus. By surface analysis, gioia + -oso.

parole.significato: to rejoice (in) or (at), or be delighted (by)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French joir. Doublet of godere.
Borrowed from Old French jornee. Documented from 1230–50. Derivable from giorno + -ata.
Borrowed from Old French joste, derived from joster.
Borrowed from Old French joster, from Vulgar Latin *iuxtāre, from Latin iuxtā (whence Italian giusta).
From Old French girfaut, gerfault.
Borrowed from Old French jolif.
From Old French guisarme, gisarme, jusarme.

parole.significato: university student (usually one with a carefree or lax way of life)
parole.testo: From Old French goliard.
Borrowed from Old French gonfalon, from Frankish *gundfano, from Proto-Germanic *gunþifanô.

parole.significato: grange (outlying land belonging to a monastery)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French grange.

Borrowed from Old French or Old Occitan, both from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz (“grey”). Akin to Old High German grīs (“grey”) (German greis) and Dutch grijs (“grey”). More at grizzle. Cognate with Sicilian grisu/griciu.
From Old French gaïm, a word of Germanic origin.
Borrowed from Old French guerrier.
From Old French guige, guiche, from Frankish *wiþþjā, from Proto-Germanic *wiþjǭ (“band, strap, cord”).
Probably borrowed from Old French broueillier. Compare French embrouiller and Sicilian mprugghiari.
From Old French maintenant, from maintenir, cognate to mantenere (“keep, maintain”), both ultimately from Late Latin manūteneō (literally “to hold by hand”).
Probably borrowed from Old French empeechier, from Late Latin impedicāre. Compare French empêcher. Doublet of impacciare and impedicare.
Borrowed from Old French empoverir.
Variant of imprentare (itself from Old French empreinte), influenced by pronto.
Borrowed from Old French emprunter and probably adapted in form to etymology 2. First attested in 1260.
From Old French a bandon.
Maybe from Old French chamoir. Compare Italian cimurro (“distemper”).
Borrowed from Old French engleis.
Either: * From an Old French word, making it cognate with the modern encombrer (“to clutter”). * Or, from Italian ingombro (“encumbrance”) + -are.
From Old French chan, from Medieval Latin chanis, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.

Borrowed from Old French lait, leit (“unpleasant, horrible, odious”), of Germanic origin, from Low Frankish *laiþ (“unpleasant, obstinate, odious”) from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz (“sorrowful, unpleasant”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“unpleasant”). Akin to Old High German leid (“unpleasant, odious

Borrowed from Old French lampe, from Latin lampada, alternative form of lampas (“lamp, lantern”), from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp or flambeau”), derived from λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”). Doublet of lampada.
From Old French liart (“grey”).
Borrowed from Old French legier, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin levis.
Adapted borrowing of French lévrier, from Old French levrer, from Late Latin canem leporārium (literally “hare dog, harehound”), from Latin lepus (“hare”). By surface analysis, lepre + -iero.
Borrowed from Old French lige; see English liege.
Borrowed from Old French loge, from Medieval Latin laubĭa, from Frankish *laubijā.
Borrowed from Old French longe.
From Old French lorgne (“crosseyed”).
From Old French lot, from Frankish *hlot, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą.
Borrowed from Old French maquerel.
Borrowed from Old French malestru, malastru, from Old Occitan malastruc, derived from mal (“bad”) + astruc (“lucky”).
From Old French malvis (“redwing”); compare French mauvis (“redwing”) and Spanish malvís.
Probably from Old French manche (“sleeve”).
Borrowed from Old French mangier, from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of manducare, manicare, and manucare.
Borrowed from Old French maniere, from manere.
Borrowed from Old French manovrer, from Vulgar Latin *manuoperāre, from Latin manu (“by hand”) + operor (“to work”).
From Old French martre.
Borrowed from Old French mastin, from Vulgar Latin *mans'tinus < *mansuetīnus (“tamed (animal)”), from Latin mānsuetus (“tamed”).
Borrowed from Old French menestrel (compare modern ménestrel), from Late Latin ministeriāle(m), from Latin ministerium.
From Old French mentevoir, from Latin mente habēre ("have in mind").
Borrowed from Old French merlanc, merlenc, derived from Latin merula.
Borrowed from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).
Borrowed from Old French menestrier a variant of ménestrel. Compare French ménétrier.
Borrowed from Old French mirabolan, from Latin myrobalanum, from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos).
From Old French mortaise, from Arabic مورتاز (murtazz, “fastened”), from راز (razza, “to cut a recess”).
Borrowed from Old French muguete.

parole.significato: a part (as yet unidentified) of armor, apparently covering the shoulders
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French musequin.
Borrowed from Old French oblier.
Borrowed from Old French outrecuidance; see -anza.
Borrowed from Old French oltrage, from Vulgar Latin *ultrāticum.
Borrowed from Old French homage, from Medieval Latin homināticum, from homo (“man”).
From Old French omelie, from Late Latin homīlia, from Ancient Greek ὁμιλία (homilía, “conversation; sermon”).
Borrowed from Old French honte, from Early Medieval Latin haunta, borrowed from Frankish *haunitha, from Proto-Germanic *hauniþō (“humiliation”).
From Old French honteux (“ashamed; shameful”). By surface analysis, onta (“shame”) + -oso (“-ous, -ful”).

parole.significato: to eavesdrop, to listen in; to overhear
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French oreillier, from oreille (“ear”). By surface analysis, orecchia + -are.
Borrowed from Old French oste (“innkeeper, landlord”), which is from Latin hospitem. From the same Latin source: Italian ospite (a doublet).
Borrowed from Old French ostel, from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospitale.
Borrowed from Old French otrier, from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre. Doublet of autorizzare.
Alteration of pelanda (“houppelande”), from Old French houppelande.

parole.significato: a long, wide domestic gaberdine-like clothing usually worn by males
parole.testo: From palandra, from former pelanda (“houppelande”), from Old French houppelande.
From Old French parc. First attested in the 14th c.
Borrowed from Old French pareil, from Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Classical Latin pār (“even, equal”). Doublet of parecchio and pariglio.
Borrowed from Old French pareil, from Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār (“even, equal”). Doublet of parecchio and pareglio.
From passare + -aggio, or from Old French passage.
From Old French peage or Old Occitan pezatge, both from Medieval Latin pedāticum, derived from Latin pes (“foot”). Modelled in Italian after piede + -aggio.
Apheresis from earlier opelanda, from Old French houppelande.

Of uncertain origin. First recorded in standard Italian in the late 19th century via Northern military conscripts. Proposed derivations include: # A Northern blend of Piedmontese plandra (“dissolute woman”) + landrone (“loafer”). # A derivative of palandrana (“loose gown”), via Old French houppeland

parole.significato: amulet of metal or stone, hung around the neck
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French pentacol.
Borrowed from Old French pardonance, derived from pardoner (“to forgive”).
Borrowed from Old French petit, from Vulgar Latin *pitittus, of probably imitative origin.

parole.significato: the floodplain areas of the river Po
parole.testo: Maybe from Old French piarda (“Celebrity”).
Borrowed from Old French posterle, from Late Latin posterula.
From earlier priscione, possibly via Old French prison, from Latin prehēnsiōnem (“the act of seizing”), from prehendō (“to seize, grab”). Doublet of prensione.
From prigione + -iero, influenced by Old French prisonier.
Semi-learned borrowing from Old French premier (“first”), from Classical Latin prīmārius (“of the first rank, chief, principal, excellent”). Doublet of primaio and primario
From Old French profit, from Latin profectus.
From Old French pulcele, pucele, first attested in the 10th century as pulcella, from Vulgar Latin *pūllicella, of disputed origin, perhaps derived from Latin pullus (“young animal”).
From Old French putain, from Latin puta (“girl”).

parole.significato: to quote (to name the current price of a financial security)
parole.testo: From quota f and influenced by Old French coter, both ultimately from Latin quota f
Borrowed from Old French ramposner or Provençal ramponar.
Borrowed from Old French reame, reaume (whence also Modern French royaume).

From Old French rifler "to scrape, scratch", from Middle High German riffeln, to scratch, heckle (flax), from Old High German riffilon "to tear by rubbing", akin to rip, ripple; see also Old English geriflian "to wrinkle," Old Norse rifa "to tear, break".
From Old French eritage.

Borrowed from Old French ribaud, ribauld (“rogue, scoundrel”), from riber (“to be licentious”), from Frankish *rīban (“to copulate, be in heat”, literally “to rub”), from Proto-Germanic *wrībaną (“to turn, twist, writhe”), from Proto-Indo-European *werp-, *werb- (“to turn, twist”).
Borrowed from Old French rime, from a Germanic word cognate with Old English rīm (“counting”).
Borrowed from Old French remembrer.
Borrowed from Old French riviere.
Borrowed from Old French roche, from Early Medieval Latin rocca, of uncertain origin. Doublet of rocca.
Borrowed from Old French rognon, itself from a Vulgar Latin *reniōnem, from Latin ren.
Borrowed from Old French romanz, which stems from the Latin expression romanice loqui (“to speak in the Roman way”). Cognate with English romance (noun).
Borrowed from Old French sage, itself from Vulgar Latin *sapium, from Latin sapiō (“to be wise”). Doublet of savio, sapio, and sapido. Compare Sicilian saviu.
Borrowed from Old French sagrin (compare modern French chagrin), from Turkish sağrı.
Borrowed from Old French saie, from Latin saga, plural of sagum (“cloak”).
Borrowed from Old French saie, from Latin sagum.
From Old French saumastre.
Borrowed from Old French sairement, from Late Latin sacrāmentum. Doublet of sacramento.
Borrowed from Old French sarge, from Vulgar Latin *sarica, from Latin sērica, ultimately from Ancient Greek σηρῐκός (sērĭkós, “silken”).
Borrowed from Old French saur.

parole.significato: to tear to pieces, to tear apart
parole.testo: From s- + brano (“piece”) + -are, or from Old French esbraoner, from braon (“slice of meat”).
From schifo (“disgust, loathing”) + -are, from Old French eschiver (“to dread, shun, avoid”).

From Old French eschiu (“shy, timid”) (cf. eschiver), from Frankish *skeuh (“shy, timid, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy, frightened”). Cognate with English shy, Sicilian schifiju (“disgust, mess”). More at shy, eschew.

parole.significato: to dodge, sidestep, avoid, or evade
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French eschiver (“to escape, avoid”).
Borrowed from Old French sentier, from Early Medieval Latin sēmitārius, derived from Latin sēmita.
From Old French sidre, from Latin sīcera, from Ancient Greek σῑ́κερᾰ (sī́keră).
Borrowed from Old French simonie.

parole.significato: king, monarch (only when addressing a sovereign)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French sire. See also sere. Doublet of signore.

parole.significato: to shine, to sparkle, to glitter (of lights and bright colors)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old French esmailler (“to enamel; to decorate with bright colors”); compare French émailler.
Borrowed from Old French esmarrir, from marir (“to frustrate, to sadden”), from Frankish *marrijan.
From Old French soie.
Borrowed from Old French somier, from Late Latin sagmarius, from Latin sagma. See also the inherited doublet somaro.
Borrowed from Old French sor-. More or less a doublet of sopra- and sovra-.

parole.significato: to overcome or surmount; to be on top of something
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French sormonter. First attested in the 14th century. By surface analysis, sor- + montare.
First attested in the 13th century. From sor- + prendere, possibly on the calque of Old French sorprendre.
Borrowed from Old French sovent, from Latin subinde. See French souvent.
From sovra, modeled after Old French soverain, Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super, whence also soprano. Cognate to French souverain, Spanish and Portuguese soberano. Doublet of soprano.

parole.significato: to rush through (homework, a job, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old French despeechier, despechier.
From Old French espiet.
Semi-learned borrowing from Old French espringale, itself derived from Frankish *springan. Cognate with German springen (“to jump”).
From Old French spole, espole, from Middle Dutch spoele, from Old Dutch *spōla, *spuola, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ (“spool”). More at spool.
Borrowed from Old French esprover.

parole.significato: a marketplace where goods had to be brought before being able to be sold elsewhere
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French estaple (“marketplace”).
Borrowed from Old French estandart.
Borrowed from Old French estophe, estoffe (compare modern French étoffe), from estoffer, from Frankish *stopfôn.
Borrowed from Old French estrief, of Germanic origin. See modern French étrier.
Borrowed from Old French estrille, from Latin strigilis.

From s- + tronzo (“blunt, dull”) (obsolete) + -are, from Old French trons, possibly of Celtic origin. Unrelated to the word stronzo (“shit-for-brains, turd”) but, since the verb is obsolete in usage, it's likely it would be mistaken as a derivative of the vulgar word.
From Old French tabart (“simple sleeveless overtunic; heavy overmantel”), of unknown origin.
Borrowed from Old French taffetas, from Medieval Latin taffata, from Persian تافته (tâfte), from تافتن.

Learned borrowing from Old French talent (“desire, wish”), from Classical Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money; (post-Classical) gift from God; (Medieval) skill, ability”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talen
From Old French tamarinde, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ (tamr hindiyy).
From Old French tumberel.
Borrowed from Old French torche, from Vulgar Latin *torca, from torqua, from Latin torquēs, torquīs (“wreath”), from torqueō (“twist”, verb).
From Old French tornoi.
Borrowed from Old French traïner, from Vulgar Latin *tragināre, from *tragere, from Latin trahere (“to drag”) (compare trarre). Doublet of trascinare, which was inherited.
From Old French travailler, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), from Late Latin tripālium (“torture device”).
Probably a blend of Old French tresce (“tress”) and trina (“sash”). Possibly influenced by tre (“three”). Compare French tresse, Sicilian trizza, Spanish trenza.
From Old French trons.
